Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Situation2: They occasionally tidy up visible clutter and do light cleaning in shared spaces.
Story: It was 2 a.m. when my phone buzzed, jolting me awake. I saw my friend’s name on the screen, and when I answered, I could barely make out her words through her sobs. She needed me—needed someone to listen, to just be there. I sat up, heart pounding, trying to focus on her voice, to offer comfort and understanding. But as I listened, my eyes drifted to the clock. In just a few hours, I was supposed to start my shift as the housekeeping cleaner. The apartment was a mess; I’d only managed to do a quick sweep of the living room before collapsing into bed. My supervisor had already warned me about missing spots and not being thorough enough. If I didn’t do a better job this time, I could lose the position. My friend’s pain pulled at me, but so did the weight of my responsibilities. I gripped the phone tighter, torn between being the friend she needed and the cleaner I was expected to be.
